questions.question: Two fraction bars are exactly the same length, and each whole bar stands for 1. Each bar is divided into 6 equal parts. Bar A has 4 of its 6 parts shaded, and Bar B has 2 of its 6 parts shaded. Which statement is true?
options: 4/6 is greater than 2/6
4/6 and 2/6 are equal, because both bars are the same length
2/6 is greater than 4/6
You cannot compare them until you change them to a common denominator
questions.explain: Both bars are cut into sixths, so every shaded part is the same size; with a common denominator you just compare the numerators, and 4 shaded parts beat 2, so 4/6 is greater. The trap is thinking you must change the denominators first, but these fractions already share one.

questions.question: A fraction bar shows one whole metre of ribbon cut into 10 equal parts. On Ribbon A, 7 of the 10 parts are shaded. On Ribbon B, 9 of the 10 parts are shaded. Which shaded amount is smaller?
options: They are the same, because both ribbons have 10 parts
questions.explain: Each part is one tenth of a metre on both ribbons, so the fraction with fewer shaded parts is smaller: 7/10 is less than 9/10. A common slip is flipping the numbers and writing the number of parts on top.

questions.question: Three fraction bars are the same length, and each whole bar stands for 1. Every bar is divided into 12 equal parts. The first bar has 5 parts shaded, the second has 11 parts shaded, and the third has 8 parts shaded. Which fraction is the greatest?
options: All three are equal, because every bar has 12 equal parts
questions.explain: Twelfths are the same size on every bar, so the greatest fraction is simply the one with the most shaded parts, 11/12. Same denominator does not mean the fractions are equal; it means the pieces are equal.

questions.question: Bar C and Bar D are the same length, and each whole bar stands for 1. Each bar is divided into 5 equal parts. Bar C has 2 parts shaded and Bar D has 3 parts shaded. Which symbol makes this true: 2/5 ___ 3/5 ?
options: No symbol works until the two bars have different denominators
questions.explain: With the same denominator, fifths, the pieces match in size, so 2 shaded pieces are fewer than 3 and 2/5 is less than 3/5. Watch the direction of the symbol: the open side always faces the larger fraction.

questions.question: Only one of these comparisons is true. Which one is it?
options: 7/9 is greater than 6/9
5/9 is less than 4/9
3/9 is equal to 4/9
2/9 is greater than 8/9
questions.explain: All of these are ninths, so the fraction with the larger numerator is larger, which makes 7/9 greater than 6/9. Fractions with the same denominator are only equal when the numerators match too.

questions.question: Maya and Liam each carry an identical 1 L water bottle marked in eighths. During a hike on the North Shore, Maya drinks 5/8 L and Liam drinks 3/8 L. Who drinks more, and why?
options: Liam, because 3 is a smaller number, so each of his parts is bigger
Maya, because the bottles are the same size and 5 eighths is more eighths than 3 eighths
They drink the same amount, because both bottles are marked in 8 equal parts
Liam, because 8 minus 3 equals 5, so his share is really 5/8 too
questions.explain: The bottles are identical and both are cut into eighths, so one eighth means the same amount for each child; compare the numerators and 5/8 beats 3/8. The 'fewer parts means bigger parts' idea is about the denominator, not the numerator.

questions.question: Ms. Chan writes these amounts of a class garden bed on the board: 7/12, 2/12, 11/12 and 5/12. Which list puts them in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Every fraction is twelfths, so ordering the fractions is the same as ordering the numerators 2, 5, 7, 11 from smallest to largest. Read the question carefully: least to greatest means you start with the smallest numerator, not the largest.

questions.question: Ella has to fill in a missing numerator on her homework so that this is true: ___/9 is less than 5/9. Which number can she write in the blank?
questions.explain: Both fractions are ninths, so the missing numerator just has to be smaller than 5, and 3 works. Writing 5 would make the two fractions equal rather than less than, which is a common mix-up.

questions.question: At a family picnic in Kelowna, a small pan of gingerbread and a large pan of gingerbread are each cut into 6 equal pieces. Noah eats 4/6 of the small pan and Emma eats 3/6 of the large pan. Which statement is correct?
options: We cannot be sure who ate more gingerbread, because the two pans are not the same size
Emma ate more, because her pan is bigger, so 3/6 must be more than 4/6
They ate the same amount, because both pans were cut into 6 equal pieces
Noah ate more gingerbread, because 4/6 is greater than 3/6
questions.explain: Comparing numerators over a common denominator only tells you which fraction is bigger when both fractions describe the same size whole; here a sixth of the large pan is bigger than a sixth of the small pan, so the amounts cannot be compared. Saying 4/6 is greater than 3/6 is true about the fractions, but not about the actual gingerbread.

questions.question: Three same-size flats of blueberries at a Richmond market are each divided into 12 equal boxes. On Saturday, stand A sold 7/12 of its flat, stand B sold 11/12 of its flat, and stand C sold 5/12 of its flat. Which stand sold the second-largest amount?
options: Stand B, with 11/12
Stand A, with 7/12
Stand C, with 5/12
You cannot tell, because 7, 11 and 5 do not share a common denominator
questions.explain: First order the twelfths by numerator, 11/12 then 7/12 then 5/12, and then pick the second one in that list, which is stand A with 7/12. The numerators do not need a common denominator; the fractions already have one, since all three flats are cut into twelfths.

questions.question: During a class discussion in Victoria, Liam says: 'Since 9/11 and 4/11 have the same denominator, the two fractions must be equal.' Which correction is best?
options: Liam is right; sharing a common denominator makes two fractions equal
The fraction with the smaller numerator is always the larger one, so 4/11 is greater than 9/11
The same denominator means the parts are the same size, so compare the numerators: 9/11 is greater than 4/11
Liam should add the denominators, 11 plus 11 equals 22, and compare 9/22 with 4/22
questions.explain: A common denominator tells you the pieces are the same size, which is exactly what lets you compare the numerators, so 9 elevenths is greater than 4 elevenths. Never add the denominators together when comparing; the denominator stays 11.

questions.question: Marcus and Jade each start with a 1 m ribbon, and each ribbon is cut into 4 equal parts. Marcus uses 2/4 m and Jade uses 3/4 m. Marcus says, 'Mine is longer, because using fewer parts means each of my parts is longer.' Who is right?
options: Marcus, because using fewer parts always makes each part longer
Neither of them; you cannot compare the lengths until the fractions have different denominators
They used the same length, because both ribbons started at 1 m
Jade, because both ribbons are cut into fourths, so every part is 1/4 m long, and 3 parts are longer than 2 parts
questions.explain: Both ribbons are the same whole cut into fourths, so each part is the same length and the child who uses more parts uses more ribbon: 3/4 m is longer than 2/4 m. The 'fewer parts means longer parts' rule is about the denominator (fourths versus eighths), not about how many parts you use.
